name: Victor of Vita
knownFor: A Catholic churchman of Vandal Africa whose History of the Persecution is the main account of how the Vandal kings Geiseric and Huneric treated the Catholic church.
dates: Wrote, he says, in the sixtieth year since the Vandals crossed into Africa. Huneric's edict, which he copies, is dated at Carthage six days before the Kalends of March; Michael Petschenig puts it in 484. No source used here gives his birth or death
place: Africa under the Vandals; Carthage; Vita

keyWorks.title: History of the Persecution in Africa
keyWorks.about: three books on the Vandal kings Geiseric and Huneric and the Catholic church, with Huneric's edicts copied in

traces: He keeps the texts of Huneric's edicts against the Catholic church.
He keeps the Book of Faith the Catholic bishops gave in to the king; Michael Petschenig thinks it likely that Victor put it into his history himself.
remembered: Procopius of Caesarea, on the tongues Huneric (his Honoric) cut out: "even up to my time were going about in Byzantium having their speech uninjured."

uncertain: Victor is a victim and an enemy of the Vandal church, and his book is polemic. He calls the Vandals a cruel and savage people and their faith the Arian heresy.
That he was bishop of Vita rests on the titles in the manuscripts of his book. He calls Pampinianus the bishop of "our city"; Karl Halm takes that to mean Vita.

That the Catholics of Tipasa still spoke after their tongues were cut out rests on Victor and on Procopius of Caesarea, who says such people were still in Byzantium in his own day. Victor names one of them, the subdeacon Reparatus, at Constantinople.
The prologue that opens his History is printed in brackets by Michael Petschenig, who counts it among the doubtful parts of the text.
No source used here tells his own life beyond what his History says, his birth or his death. He is not Victor of Tunnuna, the later African chronicler.
